cues.en: and rolling. I can't clickbait this video. I mean, I could, but it wouldn't really be fair to anyone involved. I know the title and the thumbnail aren't going to pull loads of people in, but I hope they can trust me when I say, I promise this story is really interesting. Because it is. This is one of the best things I've found while researching in years. So this starts when I'm looking up old television shows. I'm about three research tangents deep, and I find this incredible line in a newspaper article from 1997.
cues.zh: 开机了。我没法用标题党来做这个视频。我是说，我当然可以，但这真对不起涉及的所有人。我知道标题和封面吸引不来太多人，但希望大家能相信我说的话，我保证这个故事真的特别有意思。因为确实如此。这是我这几年来查资料发现的最棒的东西之一。事情开始于我在查一些老电视节目。我大概跑偏了三层相关资料，然后在一篇1997年的报纸文章里发现了这么一句不可思议的话。

cues.en: The microwave was invented to meet a need to heat hamsters humanely in 1950s laboratories. And I read that, and I thought, that's ridiculous, no it wasn't. Was it?
cues.zh: 微波炉的发明是为了满足1950年代实验室人道加热仓鼠的需求。我看到这句的时候想，太扯了吧，怎么可能。难道是真的？

cues.en: There's a well-known story about the engineer who invented the microwave. Percy Spencer, just after World War II, was working on one of the new military-grade radars while it was active, and he realised that the peanut bar in his back pocket had melted. Which implies that the radar also nearly cooked part of him as well. Unshielded radars are really dangerous, but it was the 1940s. The attitude to safety was a bit more lax. Now, it wasn't a surprise that electromagnetic radiation...
cues.zh: 关于发明微波炉的工程师，有一个广为人知的故事。二战刚结束后，Percy Spencer 在一台处于工作状态的新型军用雷达旁工作，这时他发现自己后兜里的花生糖融化了。这也意味着，雷达差点把他也烤熟了一部分。没有屏蔽保护的雷达非常危险，但那可是1940年代。大家对安全防范的态度要松懈得多。话说回来，电磁辐射其实并不让人感到意外……

cues.en: could heat stuff. That had been known for a while. People had actually been using it for medical therapies for a while. Different wavelengths had different effects. But Percy Spencer was the first person to realise you could cook efficiently with wavelengths that were put out by radar, and then realise that you could sell that, and then realise, well, I could turn that into a usable product.
cues.zh: 能加热东西。这事大家早就知道了。人们甚至早就用它来进行医疗了。不同的波长有不同的效果。但 Percy Spencer 是第一个意识到可以用雷达发射的波长来高效烹饪的人，随后他又意识到这可以卖钱，接着又意识到，嘿，我能把它做成实用的产品。

cues.en: because a massive radar dish is basically the same technology as this microwave. I'm not going to try and take this thing apart, I'm not qualified, and there is a high-voltage capacitor in here which can carry enough charge to kill. Don't mess about with these unless you know what you're doing. But inside here is...
cues.zh: 因为巨大的雷达天线和这台微波炉基本上用的是同一种技术。我可不敢拆开这玩意儿，我没那资格，而且里面有个高压电容，存的电量足以致命。除非你非常专业，否则千万别乱拆。但在这里面其实是……

cues.en: Inside here, in the bit you can't access, there's a microwave generator called a magnetron. It moves an electric current past a big magnet with a hole in it, and because physics, that produces electromagnetic radiation. To tune the size of the hole in the magnet, you get different frequencies of radiation. The best analogy I've found is that it's like blowing air over glass bottles and changing the pitch by changing the amount of water inside. So... that, but with electricity.
cues.zh: 在这里面你碰不到的地方，有一个叫磁控管的微波发生器。它让电流穿过一个带孔的大磁铁，因为物理学原理，这样就会产生电磁辐射。调节磁铁上孔的大小，就能得到不同频率的辐射。我能找到的最佳类比是，这就像往玻璃瓶口吹气，通过改变里面的水量来改变音调。所以……差不多就是那样，只是换成了电。

cues.en: Look, I don't have a physics degree. Long story short, a magnetron converts electricity into electromagnetic radiation. You send pulses of that radiation out into the sky and you listen for the echoes, you've got radar, and you've helped win World War II. Or you could put a magnetron inside a safe radiation-proof box called a Faraday cage, you tune the wavelength so that water absorbs the radiation easily, and you've got a microwave, and you can cook lunch. The technical term is diathermic heating.
cues.zh: 听着，我又没有物理学学位。长话短说，磁控管就是把电能转化为电磁辐射。把这种辐射的脉冲发射到空中，然后监听回波，你就得到了雷达，顺便帮着打赢了二战。或者，你也可以把磁控管放进一个叫法拉第笼的安全防辐射盒子里，调好波长让水分子容易吸收辐射，你就得到了一台微波炉，能拿来做午饭了。专业术语叫“透热加热”。

cues.en: And less than a year after the melting peanut bar incident, which could so easily have been like the cooked hand incident, or worse, but less than a year after that, that engineer's company, Defence Contractor Raytheon, they released the first commercial microwave. It was called the Radar Range, it was the size of a fridge, it had to be actively cooled, it was incredibly expensive, and it was designed for big commercial kitchens. That was 1947.
cues.zh: 而在花生糖融化事件发生后不到一年——那次意外本极有可能像手被烤熟那样严重，甚至更糟——但在那之后不到一年，那位工程师所在的公司，国防承包商 Raytheon，就推出了第一款商用微波炉。它被称为 Radar Range，有冰箱那么大，必须进行主动冷却，价格极其昂贵，而且是专为大型商用厨房设计的。那是 1947 年。

cues.en: The first microwave was, we'd know it today, a cheap box that you plug in. That was from the late 1960s, once magnetron technology had moved on a bit. At no point in that well-referenced, well-known story does anyone mention heating hamsters in laboratories in the 1950s. So that should be pretty easy to disprove, right? It's going to be an urban legend. There are a lot of urban legends like that.
cues.zh: 而我们今天所熟知的第一款微波炉，也就是插上电就能用的小型廉价盒子，是在 1960 年代后期才出现的，那时磁控管技术已经有了进一步发展。在这个引证详实、广为人知的故事里，从始至终都没有人提到过 1950 年代在实验室里加热仓鼠的事。所以这应该很容易被证伪，对吧？它肯定是个都市传说。毕竟这类都市传说可太多了。

cues.en: So I started doing some journal searches, and pretty quickly I found papers from the 1950s talking about the reanimation of frozen rats and hamsters. Those papers were written by scientists at the National Institute for Medical Research, a government laboratory in Mill Hill in suburban north London, about half a mile that way. I would have filmed closer to that, but unfortunately it was pulled down a few years ago and the whole area is now a load of new-build housing. Anyway, National Institute for Medical Research. In the 1950s, that research included cryobiology, the effects of extreme cold on body...
cues.zh: 于是我开始检索一些期刊，很快就找到了20世纪50年代关于复活冷冻大鼠和仓鼠的论文。这些论文出自英国国家医学研究院（National Institute for Medical Research）的科学家之手，那是位于伦敦北部郊区 Mill Hill 的一家政府实验室，顺着那个方向走大概半英里就是。我本想离得更近一些拍，但不幸的是，它几年前就被拆除了，那一整片地方现在全是新建的住宅。不管怎样，这家国家医学研究院，在20世纪50年代的研究涵盖了低温生物学，也就是极度严寒对身体……

cues.en: and tissue. Scientists at that lab froze rats and hamsters beyond the point of death. They use ice and a bath of propylene glycol, which is airplane de-icer held at below zero, and at that point the animal is dead and will not recover on its own. No heart rate, no breathing, core temperature around one degree Celsius, somewhere between 10 and 50% of the animal's body water, frozen to ice.
cues.zh: 以及组织的影响。那家实验室的科学家将大鼠和仓鼠冷冻到彻底死亡的状态。他们使用的是冰块以及零度以下的丙二醇浴（也就是飞机除冰剂），到了那个阶段，动物已经死亡，无法自行苏醒。没有心率，没有呼吸，核心体温在大约摄氏1度左右，体内有10%到50%的水分都结成了冰。

cues.en: And then, by applying hot spatulas to the chest, or high-intensity hot beams of light, the researchers would try to warm the animals up and bring them back to life. The success rate wasn't great, and the animals were often left with burns, but it did sometimes work. We'll get to why they were doing that later, but by 1955, one of the researchers has the idea to use a magnetron, reasoning that it'd be a lot more safe and humane to reheat the whole animal at once, rather than risk burning it. Actually, I say one of the researchers, there's a name on that paper that might be a bit familiar.
cues.zh: 接着，研究人员会用发烫的抹刀按在胸口，或者用高强度的热光束照射，试图让动物回温复活。成功率不算高，动物还经常被烫伤，但有时确实管用。我们稍后再聊他们为什么要这么做，不过到了1955年，其中一位研究人员想到了使用磁控管，他觉得一次性给整只动物加热，不仅更安全也更人道，还能避免烫伤的风险。其实，说是其中一位研究人员，那篇论文上有一个名字大家可能听着有点耳熟。

cues.en: James Lovelock, one of the last independent scientists, born in 1919, back when scientists could be an entire job description rather than botanist or physicist or computational linguist. Someone who worked across disciplines on whatever they found interesting, or whatever they were hired to do.
cues.zh: James Lovelock，最后几位独立科学家之一，生于1919年，那会儿“科学家”本身就可以是一份完整的职业描述，而不是非得细分植物学家、物理学家或计算语言学家。他是个跨学科工作的人，什么有趣就研究什么，或者受雇做什么就做什么。

cues.en: Lovelock is best known for inventing Gaia theory, the idea of Earth as a self-regulating system. He also invented the electron capture detector, which found CFCs in the atmosphere and helped discover the ozone hole. Hardware that he helped design for NASA is sitting on Mars, because it landed there with the Viking probes in 1976. And one of the earlier projects in his career, back in the 1950s, was at the National Institute for Medical Research, freezing rats and hamsters. And he had the idea to use microwave diathermy... diathermy? Diath...
cues.zh: Lovelock 最广为人知的成就是提出了盖亚假说，即把地球看作一个自我调节的系统。他还发明了电子捕获检测器，在大气中检测到了氟氯烃，并助力发现了臭氧层空洞。他协助 NASA 设计的硬件如今就留在火星上，因为它们早在 1976 年就随维京号探测器着陆了。而在他职业生涯早期的 1950 年代，他曾在英国国家医学研究所工作，负责冷冻大鼠和仓鼠。当时他萌生了一个想法，用微波透热疗法……透热？透……

cues.en: Dias enemy. To reheat them. But the papers and anecdotes from back then all seem to contradict each other. The timeline is difficult to piece together. There are reliable sources with completely different stories and claims. So I went to ask him about it. Do you know you're the first person to come and ask me about the freezing wet? Because James Lovelock, at 101 years old, lives somewhere vaguely round here on the south coast of England, goes for a walk along the coast every day, and was happy to be interviewed.
cues.zh: 透敌。用它来复温。但当年的那些论文和轶事似乎全都互相矛盾。时间线很难拼凑完整。不同可靠来源的说法和主张完全大相径庭。所以我决定亲自去问问他。“你知道吗，你是第一个跑来问我关于冷冻大鼠的人。”因为 101 岁高龄的 James Lovelock，就住在英格兰南海岸的大致某个地方，每天都会沿海岸散步，而且很乐意接受采访。

cues.en: One biologist, Audrey Smith, was able to revive a hamster that had been frozen. When they woke up, they got a gigantic burn all across their chest, and that must have been pretty painful. And it was messy. I thought, this is a lousy way to do it. So I said, why don't you use diocermic potentialings of my own money. I bought a surplus RAF transmitter.
cues.zh: 生物学家 Audrey Smith 曾成功复活过一只被冻僵的仓鼠。但在苏醒时，仓鼠胸前留下了大片严重灼伤，那肯定非常痛苦。现场也是一团糟。我想，这种方法太糟糕了。所以我说，为什么不用透热疗法呢？于是我自掏腰包，买了一台皇家空军退役的发射机。

cues.en: joined it up and sure enough it poured out 30 watts at 30 megahertz which was just about right and I took it into the lab the next day and I said look here's your diaphragm. I thought this is very untidy, made some inquiries and sure enough there were 10 centimeter magnetrons that had been invented by Booth and Randall at Birmingham University during the war. To get hold of one of those is not easy.
cues.zh: 把它接好后，果然在 30 兆赫下输出了 30 瓦的功率，正好合适。第二天我把它带到实验室说，看，这是你们要的透热装置。我觉得这还是太笨重杂乱了，便四处打听，果不其然，找到了二战期间伯明翰大学的 Booth 和 Randall 发明的 10 厘米磁控管。不过想搞到一台可没那么容易。

cues.en: And this is where being in the government department helped a bit. So I just made a few inquiries, how do I get home? And they said, oh, they're working on them down at just above Portsmouth. I said, any chance of borrowing one of your magnetrons? And he said, oh, no. He said, we can give you one if you want. It's an interesting cause. Why not? I've joined this up with a wave guide into a metal box.
cues.zh: 这时候在政府部门工作就派上点用场了。我打听了一下，该怎么搞到手？他们说，在朴茨茅斯往北一点的地方有人在研究这玩意儿。我问，能借你们一个磁控管用用吗？对方说，借什么借，你要的话我们直接送你一个。这事挺有意思的，为什么不呢？我就用波导管把这东西和一个金属箱连了起来。

cues.en: It wasn't so much a box, it was just a thing made out of chicken wire, except it's finer than chicken wire, a bit closer mesh. And that was just like the box of a microwave oven. And I fed the microwave into it, and I told Audrey, now put your hamster in there. That's a microwave. James Lovock may not have invented the first microwave, but he certainly invented a microwave. The idea of using magnetrons to heat stuff wasn't his, but...
cues.zh: 其实也不太算箱子，就是个用铁丝网做的玩意儿，不过网孔比普通铁丝网更细更密。那感觉就像微波炉的内胆。我把微波导入进去，然后对奥黛丽说，现在把你的仓鼠放进去吧。这就是微波炉了。詹姆斯·洛夫洛克也许没有发明第一台微波炉，但他确实独立做出了一台微波炉。利用磁控管加热东西的想法虽然不是他首创的，但是……

cues.en: No one else was putting one in a Faraday cage box on a desktop. Big commercial microwaves for restaurant kitchens aren't the same thing, and besides, they weren't even on sale in the UK until a few years later. I put a potato in it and baked it, and it was perfectly all right. The safety procedures were occasionally a bit lax by modern standards. In the course of the experiments while we were building it, the thing was running open.
cues.zh: 当时没人把这种东西放在桌面的法拉第笼箱子里。餐厅厨房用的大型商用微波炉完全不是一回事，况且，英国也是几年后才开始销售那种机器。我放了个土豆进去烤，结果烤得非常好。按现在的标准来看，当时的安全规范有时确实有点松懈。我们在制作它的实验过程中，这东西一直是敞开运行的。

cues.en: and the radiation was bouncing all round the room and the light bulbs would light up without warning. The filament just had the same wavelength as the radiation and it would absorb it and light up. And pound notes were the funniest ones, they would catch fire because the metal strip inside was just about the wavelength of the magnetron.
cues.zh: 辐射在整个房间里到处反弹，灯泡会毫无预兆地亮起来。灯丝的尺寸恰好和辐射波长一致，吸收了辐射就会发亮。最搞笑的是英镑纸币，它们会直接着火，因为里面的金属安全线长度刚好差不多是磁控管的波长。

cues.en: And here's the really amazing thing. It worked. We put the hamster in there, frozen solid. And I mean frozen solid, it was like a bit of wood when you dropped it on the bench. It turned the thing up to full power on the microwave, which was, it was about a kilowatt coming out of it. And there was a timer, and after so many seconds,
cues.zh: 最神奇的地方来了。它成功了。我们把仓鼠放了进去，已经冻得硬邦邦的。我说的硬邦邦，是掉在实验台上就像块木头一样。微波炉开到最大功率，大概有一千瓦的输出。上面有个定时器，过了几十秒，

cues.en: The hamster woke up and started wandering around. Do I need to say don't try this at home? I mean, there are enough people of all ages watching that statistically, yes, I do need to say it, don't try this at home. It's unnecessary cruelty, you won't be doing medical research, you'll be doing a crime. Context is really important. But also...
cues.zh: 仓鼠醒了过来，开始四处走动。我还用说“请勿在家模仿”吗？我的意思是，看视频的各年龄段观众太多了，从概率上讲，是的，我必须得说：千万别在家里试。这是不必要的虐待，你这不是在做医学研究，你这是在犯罪。语境非常重要。但话说回来……

cues.en: But the research has been done. More than 50 years ago, there are charts of survival rate and heating. And it turns out that with a microwave, because that's what this was, with a precise, calibrated microwave and with artificial respiration to start pumping oxygen around that body, almost every rodent they froze was successfully reanimated. That's the word that the biologists used. Reanimation. Healthy. Behaving as usual. And given a retirement at an animal home, according to one of the papers. Back from being frozen to death. Sometimes multiple times.
cues.zh: 这项研究其实早就有人做过了。50多年前，就有关于加热和存活率的图表。事实证明，用一台微波炉——因为那本质上就是台微波炉——一台经过精确校准的微波炉，再加上人工呼吸把氧气泵入体内，几乎所有被他们冻僵的啮齿动物都成功复活了。生物学家用的就是这个词：复活。健康、活动如常。而且据其中一篇论文称，它们后来还被送到动物之家安享晚年。从冻死的状态中起死回生。有时甚至经历了好几次。

cues.en: So the last question is, why? Well this could be of immense importance to medicine itself for preserving tissues for transfer and also for blood transfusions because at the moment blood is kept at the blood bank for three weeks and then thrown down the sink. Imagine if that had worked on bigger animals. Back then humanity did not know what the limits were. This was an open question.
cues.zh: 所以最后一个问题是，为什么？这对医学本身可能具有极其重大的意义，无论是用于保存移植组织，还是用于输血；因为目前血库里的血液只能保存三周，之后就得倒进水槽扔掉。想象一下，如果这在更大的动物身上也能奏效呢。那时候人类还不知道极限在哪里。这还是一个悬而未决的问题。

cues.en: And the reason that all those 1960s science fiction writers and comic book authors had people being frozen in time or astronauts being sent off in cryosleep? Well, it might be because, for a little while, it looked like that might actually be possible. If freezing and diathermic reheating worked on hamsters, then maybe it'd work on rabbits. If it worked on rabbits, then maybe it'd work on primates. And if it worked on primates, then maybe it'd work on humans. It didn't. Unfortunately, it doesn't scale up. You cannot freeze a human.
cues.zh: 那为什么20世纪60年代的科幻小说家和漫画作者，都会写人们被时间冻结，或者宇航员在冷冻休眠中被发射出去呢？嗯，这可能是因为，有那么一阵子，这看起来似乎真的可行。如果冷冻和透热复温能在仓鼠身上奏效，那说不定在兔子身上也能行。如果在兔子身上行得通，那说不定灵长类动物也可以。如果灵长类动物行，那说不定人类也可以。但事实并非如此。遗憾的是，它无法拓展到更大体型。你无法冷冻一个人类。

cues.en: It's partly a matter of how quickly you can get the antifreeze agent to diffuse into the cells. Humans too big. It's just a matter of size. A hamster is an acceptable size. Sometimes research hits a brick wall. Find out a neat thing about hamsters? Check. Casually invent a microwave and then don't commercialise it? Check. Find a way to safely send astronauts to other planets.
cues.zh: 这在一定程度上取决于你能多快让防冻剂渗透到细胞里。人太大了。这纯粹是个体型问题。仓鼠的大小正合适。有时候科研就是会碰壁。发现仓鼠身上的神奇之处？搞定了。顺手发明了微波炉却没拿去商业化？搞定了。找到一种能安全把宇航员送上其他星球的方法？

cues.en: Not this time, unfortunately. But the researchers tried, and it feels like a story that shouldn't be buried as a vague anecdote in a newspaper from years ago. I think in an awful lot of science, where there's a success, it's not a scientific thing. It's an invention, which is something quite different. And I think, personally, I'm much more of an inventor than a scientist.
cues.zh: 很遗憾，这次没成。但研究人员确实努力过了，我觉得这个故事不该被埋没在多年前报纸上一段语焉不详的轶事里。我认为在许多科学领域中，所谓的成功往往并非科学本身的突破。那是一种发明，是完全不同的两码事。而我个人觉得，比起科学家，我更像是一个发明家。

cues.en: My thanks to James Lovelock for his time. His latest book, Nova Scene, is part memoir and part look to the future, and there's a link to it in the description. Oh, that was a mistake. That I... That's going to be a nightmare to watch. All right, well, I guess I don't get a second take. I put that on low.
cues.zh: 非常感谢 James Lovelock 抽出宝贵的时间。他的新书《Nova Scene》既是一部回忆录，也是对未来的展望，简介里有购买链接。哎呀，刚才弄错了。我……这看起来肯定很糟糕。好吧，看来我是没机会重录了。我把火开小点。
